title: Hotel Room or Suite for a Family Stay in Phuket?
content:
A hotel room or a suite can suit a family stay for different reasons. The useful comparison is how your confirmed party will use the space: sleeping, getting ready, storing luggage and relaxing between outings. A larger floor area can change the daily routine, while permitted occupancy and bedding still need a separate answer.

At Royal Phuket City Hotel, Premier rooms and suites offer different listed sizes. This guide compares those choices through practical family situations, so you can decide which questions matter before enquiring. The family hotel page covers the broader family-stay offering and basic booking requirements.

What does the room-size comparison tell you?

The hotel lists Premier Superior rooms at 30 sqm and Premier Deluxe rooms at 38 sqm. The Suite is 64 sqm and the Executive Suite is 75 sqm. Those figures help you compare available space; they do not say how many guests your booking permits.

Scroll sideways to compare all the room options.

ChoiceListed areaDecision to explore
Premier Superior30 sqmA room-based routine with the bedding your party can confirm
Premier Deluxe38 sqmWhether the additional room area helps with your daily needs
Suite64 sqmHow the bedroom and separate living room support your routine
Executive Suite75 sqmWhether the bedroom and living/dining area are useful to your stay

The Suite page describes a separate living room, and the Executive Suite page describes living and dining space alongside the bedroom. Review the photographs and ask about the exact proposed arrangement, rather than choosing by area alone.

When might a Premier room fit the plan?

Imagine a family whose confirmed sleeping arrangement suits a Premier room and whose days are mostly spent outside. They may want a straightforward place to get ready, leave their bags and return after dinner. For that routine, extra sitting space may be less important than the room arrangement and the rate details.

Compare the 30 sqm and 38 sqm options by thinking about the items you will actually bring. Bags, clothing and a pushchair can affect how the room feels during the stay. Ask the team how your confirmed bedding and belongings would fit into the proposed layout.

This is a planning scenario, not a statement that every family can stay in either room. Begin with the number of adults and each child's age, then ask which arrangement is permitted for your dates.

When is suite living space useful?

Now consider a family that expects to return between outings, organise belongings or spend more of the evening indoors. A separate living area can be relevant to that routine. It gives you a different layout to assess, even when it does not change the permitted sleeping arrangement.

Think about what the space would do for you. Would it help when preparing for dinner, relaxing after a town outing or keeping bags away from the bedroom? Ask how the bedroom and living area are connected and which features are part of the proposed category.

A suite's sitting area should not be treated as an extra bedroom or a promised sleeping place. The Suite and Executive Suite pages list up to two guests in their standard details. For any different party arrangement, get a specific response from reservations before making the booking.

How should you compare one suite with separate rooms?

For relatives travelling together, separate rooms may be another option to discuss. They can give different members of the group their own sleeping arrangement, while a suite may give one confirmed party more living space. These choices answer different needs.

Collect the preferences first: who wants to share, who keeps a different bedtime and whether proximity between rooms is important. Ask the hotel what it can confirm. A request for connecting or nearby rooms needs its own response; it is not established by selecting a particular category.

Compare the complete arrangements rather than two headline prices. The relevant difference includes the room allocation, confirmed bedding and items in each rate. Keep the comparison tied to your real dates and party.

What everyday details can change the decision?

Review the bathroom information for the proposed room and ask about a feature important to your family. A room photograph helps you understand one example, but a particular bathing arrangement should be checked when it affects the booking.

Meal planning also matters. Check the written rate for each guest's breakfast arrangement and ask about relevant conditions. Review the hotel dining options if you want a separate restaurant meal, then confirm the reservation and any essential requests through the venue.

Finally, compare the base with your itinerary. Royal Phuket City is in Phuket Town. If you plan to return between activities, consider those journeys alongside the room layout. Our Phuket Town or Patong guide covers the city and beach tradeoffs.

Use a simple comparison brief

  • Give your dates, adults and children's ages.
  • Describe your preferred sleeping arrangement.
  • Explain whether separate sitting space would change your routine.
  • Ask which Premier room, suite or room allocation can be confirmed.
  • Compare the layout, bedding and rate inclusions in writing.

For example, you can say: “We expect to return during the afternoon and would like to compare a confirmed room arrangement with a suite that has living space. Please explain the options for our party and dates.” That gives the team a reason behind the preference.

Quick answers about rooms and suites

Does a suite automatically sleep more people?

No. Floor area and living space are different from permitted occupancy and bedding. Confirm the actual party arrangement with reservations.

Should every family choose the largest room?

Choose according to the layout you will use and the booking the hotel can confirm. More space is useful when it supports your routine.

Where can I compare the current options?

Start with the rooms and suites overview, review the category pages and contact Royal Phuket City with your party details and preferences.
